The Battle of Agincourt. On the twenty-fifth of October, fourteen fifteen, one of the greatest military upsets in history took place near the village of Agincourt in northern France, during the Hundred Years' War. An English army under King Henry V, numbering around six thousand, defeated a much larger French force of between twenty and thirty thousand troops. The victory was built on disciplined tactics and the devastating effectiveness of the English longbow.

English forces were heavily outnumbered, but the battlefield itself became their greatest advantage. The heavy mud combined with the weight of French armour created a catastrophic bottleneck. French cavalry charges were broken before they could engage, devastated by waves of arrow fire from English archers. Henry V personally led the charge and maintained strict military discipline throughout. After capturing thousands of French nobility, he ordered their execution to prevent a counterattack and preserve his position on the battlefield.

The mud, the mud, and more mud—this alone may have decided the day. The victory gave England a temporary upper hand in the Hundred Years' War and emboldened Henry's claims to the French crown. The battle became iconic in English culture, immortalised centuries later in Shakespeare's Henry V as a triumph of will and martial virtue. It exemplified a fundamental shift in medieval warfare, where ranged weaponry and disciplined infantry proved superior to the armoured cavalry charge that had dominated the medieval battlefield for centuries.
